source: Ya'aqov - The Hebrew Epistle of James v2.0

verses.translation: And now, you rich{H6223}: cry out{H6817} and weep{H1058} over the evil{H7451} that shall come{H935} upon you.
Your riches{H6239} have rotted{H7539} and your garments{H8071} have become moth-eaten{H6211}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses simloteikhem (your garments, H8071 simlah) and ka'ash (like a moth, H6211). This echoes Isaiah 50:9 (hen kullam kabbeged yivlu ash yokhelem -- behold, all of them shall wear out like a garment, the moth shall eat them) and Isaiah 51:8. The moth-garment combination is a Hebrew prophetic image.
textual_notes: Isaiah 50:9, 51:8: The moth-eating-garments image as divine judgment on the self-assured.

verses.translation: And your silver{H3701} and your gold{H2091} shall corrode, and this shall be a testimony{H5715} for you, and it shall eat{H398} your flesh{H1320} like fire{H784}; and you store up{H6908} riches{H6239} in the end{H319} of days{H3117}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses acharit hayamim (end of days, H319/H3117) -- the fixed Hebrew eschatological formula (Gen 49:1, Deut 4:30, Isa 2:2, Mic 4:1, Dan 10:14). Greek has en eschatais hemerais (in the last days). While similar, the Hebrew term is a fixed prophetic expression with deep OT roots, not a casual time reference.
textual_notes: Genesis 49:1: Gather yourselves, that I may tell you what shall befall you be'acharit hayamim (in the end of days).

verses.translation: See{H7200}! The wage{H6468} of the hired worker{H7916} that lodges{H3885} with you cries{H6817} before{H6440} me, and their outcries{H6818} have come before{H6440} the ears{H241} of the Lord{H113} of Hosts{H6635}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses pe'ulat sachir shetalin (the wage of the hired worker that lodges with you) -- a DIRECT allusion to Leviticus 19:13: lo talin pe'ulat sachir ittekha ad boqer (the wage of a hired worker shall not lodge with you until morning). The Hebrew preserves the exact Torah vocabulary: pe'ulah (wage), sachir (hired worker), talin (lodge overnight). Greek has ho misthos ton ergaton (the wages of the workers) -- generic. No back-translator from Greek would produce the specific Lev 19:13 phrase.

Uses Tsevaot (Hosts, H6635) -- the divine title YHWH Tsevaot (YHWH of Hosts/Armies), appearing 285 times in the OT. Greek has kuriou Sabaoth -- a TRANSLITERATION of the Hebrew, showing the Greek translator did not translate but borrowed the Hebrew word. This confirms Hebrew priority for this title.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: pe'ulat sachir shetalin (Lev 19:13 vocabulary). Greek: ho misthos ton ergaton (generic wages of workers).
textual_notes: Leviticus 19:13: lo ta'ashoq et re'akha velo tigzol lo talin pe'ulat sachir ittekha ad boqer. Also Deuteronomy 24:14-15.

verses.translation: And you have had desires{H8378} of this world{H5769} and rejoiced{H8055} to the sound{H6963} of the pipe{H5748}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses ugav (pipe/organ, H5748) -- the musical instrument from Genesis 4:21: hu hayah avi kol tofes kinnor ve'ugav (he was the father of all who play the harp and pipe). Greek has etruphesate espatalesesate epi tes ges (you have lived in luxury and pleasure upon the earth) -- NO musical instrument at all. A back-translator from Greek's generic luxury/pleasure would never introduce the specific Genesis 4:21 musical instrument. The ugav connects the self-indulgent rich to the pre-Flood civilization of Cain's descendants.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: rejoiced to the sound of the ugav (pipe, Gen 4:21). Greek: you have lived in luxury and pleasure. No musical instrument in Greek.
textual_notes: Genesis 4:21: Jubal was the father of all who play the kinnor and ugav. The ugav is associated with the pre-Flood Cainite civilization.

verses.translation: And you condemn{H2803} the righteous{H6662} and kill{H4191} him, and he does not protest{H4745} against you.

translation_notes: Hatsedek (the righteous one) may refer to Yeshua, as in Acts 3:14, 7:52, 22:14.

verses.translation: And now, brothers{H251} beloved{H157}, let your hope{H8615} be upon the future from the Lord{H113}. See{H7200}! The master{H1167} of the field{H7704} waits{H6822} for the fruits{H6529} of the land{H776}, and his hope{H8615} is upon the early rain{H3138} and the latter rain{H4456}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses yoreh umalqosh (early rain and latter rain, H3138/H4456) -- the specific Hebrew agricultural-calendar terms for the autumn rains (October-November) and spring rains (March-April). Greek has proimon kai opsimon (early and late) -- generic temporal words. The Hebrew preserves the Torah's exact terminology from Deuteronomy 11:14 (venatatti metar artsekhem be'itto yoreh umalqosh) and Joel 2:23. No back-translator from the generic Greek early/late would independently produce the specialized agricultural Hebrew terms yoreh and malqosh.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: yoreh umalqosh (specific agricultural rain terms). Greek: proimon kai opsimon (generic early and late).
translation_notes: The yoreh (early rain) softens the ground for plowing and planting; the malqosh (latter rain) brings the crops to maturity before harvest. Both are necessary for the harvest -- a metaphor for patient endurance.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 11:14: I will give the rain of your land in its season, the yoreh and the malqosh. Joel 2:23: He has given you the yoreh righteously, and he will cause the rain to come down for you, the yoreh and the malqosh.

verses.translation: And you also strengthen{H2388} your hearts{H3824}, for the future from the Lord{H113} is near{H7138}.
Do not groan{H584} against each other, brothers{H251} beloved{H157}, lest you come to stumbling{H4383}, for the judge{H8199} stands{H5975} before{H6440} the door{H6607}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses shofet (judge, H8199) -- the OT title for Israel's leaders (Judges 2:16) and for YHWH himself (Gen 18:25 -- hashofet kol ha'arets, the judge of all the earth). Greek has ho krites.

verses.translation: Brothers{H251} beloved{H157}, take{H3947} for yourselves as an example the afflictions{H6869} and the endurance{H5450} of the prophets{H5030} who spoke{H1696} to you in the name{H8034} of the Lord{H113}.

See{H7200}, we praise{H7623} those who endured{H5445}. And the endurance{H5450} of Iyov{H347} you have heard{H8085}, and the end{H5490} from the Lord{H113} you have seen{H7200}, for the Lord{H113} is a God{H410} of compassion{H7356} and abundant{H7227} in lovingkindness{H2617}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses el rachamim verav chesed (God of compassion and abundant lovingkindness, H410/H7356/H7227/H2617). This echoes the divine self-revelation at Sinai in Exodus 34:6: YHWH YHWH el rachum vechanun... verav chesed (YHWH, YHWH, a God compassionate and gracious... and abundant in lovingkindness). Greek has polusplagchnos estin ho kurios kai oiktirmon (the Lord is very compassionate and merciful) -- different vocabulary. The Hebrew preserves the Exodus 34:6 formula.
Direct reference to Iyov (Job, H347) -- confirming the Job connection established in 1:12 (the verbatim Job 5:17 quote). The epistle forms an inclusio with Job.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: el rachamim verav chesed (Exodus 34:6 formula). Greek: polusplagchnos kai oiktirmon.
textual_notes: Exodus 34:6: YHWH YHWH el rachum vechanun erekh appayim verav chesed ve'emet.

verses.translation: But above{H6440} all{H3605}, brothers{H251} beloved{H157}, do not swear{H7650}, not by the heavens{H8064} or by the earth{H776} or by any oath{H7621}; but let your words{H1697} be yes{H2005} yes{H2005} and no no, so that you do not stumble{H3782}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses hen hen velav lav (yes yes and no no). Hen is Hebrew for yes/behold; lav is Aramaic/rabbinic Hebrew for no. This natural Hebrew-Aramaic code-switching is impossible to produce by back-translation from Greek's nai nai ou ou (yes yes no no, both Greek words).
greek_deviations: Hebrew mixes Hebrew (hen) and Aramaic (lav) naturally. Greek uses only Greek words (nai, ou).

verses.translation: And if one{H259} among you suffers{H5445} anything, he must pray{H6419}; and if one{H259} among you has a good{H2896} heart{H3820}, he must sing{H2167} psalms{H8416}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses lezamer tehillim (to sing psalms, H2167/H8416) -- the specific Hebrew worship vocabulary. Tehillim is the Hebrew name for the Book of Psalms. Greek has psalletho (let him sing psalms) which derives from the Hebrew concept.

verses.translation: And if one{H259} is sick{H2470}, he must call{H7121} the elders{H2205} of the congregation{H5712}, and they shall make prayer{H8605} for him and anoint{H4886} him with oil{H8081} in the name{H8034} of the Lord{H113}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses edah (congregation, H5712) -- the specific OT term for the assembly of Israel (Ex 12:3, 16:1, Num 1:2). Greek has ekklesias (church/assembly). The Hebrew preserves the Torah's communal vocabulary.

Uses mashach (anoint, H4886) -- the specific verb for priestly/royal anointing (Ex 28:41, 1 Sam 10:1, 16:13). Greek has aleipsantes (having anointed with oil). The Hebrew verb carries priestly overtones.

verses.translation: And the prayer{H8605} of faith{H530} shall help{H5826} the sick{H2470}, and the Lord{H113} shall raise him up{H6965}; and if he has sinned{H2398}, his sins{H2399} shall be forgiven{H4229}.

And confess{H3034} your sins{H2403} one{H259} to another, and each one{H259} shall make prayer{H8605} for his companion{H2270}: for YHWH{H3068} is near{H7138} to all{H3605} who call upon him{H7121}, to all{H3605} who call upon him{H7121} in truth{H571}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The second half of this verse is VERBATIM from Psalm 145:18: karov YHWH lekhol qor'av lekhol asher yiqra'uhu be'emet (YHWH is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth). Greek James 5:16 says polu ischuei deesis dikaiou energoumene (the effective prayer of a righteous man avails much) -- COMPLETELY DIFFERENT CONTENT. The Hebrew quotes a Psalm; the Greek has a generic proverb about prayer. NO back-translator from the Greek proverb would independently produce a verbatim Psalm 145:18 quotation. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire epistle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: quotes Psalm 145:18 verbatim. Greek: has a generic proverb about effective prayer. Entirely different content.
translation_notes: The Psalm 145:18 quote transforms the meaning of the verse: confession and prayer work because YHWH is NEAR to those who call in truth.
textual_notes: Psalm 145:18: karov YHWH lekhol qor'av lekhol asher yiqra'uhu be'emet.

verses.translation: And Eliyahu{H452} the prophet{H5030} was a man{H120} like us, and he made prayer{H8605} that rain{H1653} should not come{H935}, and rain{H1653} did not come{H935} upon the land{H776} three{H7969} years{H8141} and a half{H2677}.

textual_notes: 1 Kings 17-18 narrates Elijah's prayer and the drought.

verses.translation: And afterward he made prayer{H8605} that rain{H1653} should come{H935}, and the heavens{H8064} gave{H5414} their waters{H4325} and the land{H776} gave its fruit{H6529}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses shamayim et meimam ve'ha-arets et piryah (the heavens their waters and the land its fruit) -- natural Hebrew paired construction of heaven and earth giving their produce. This is standard OT agricultural blessing language (Deut 28:4,12; Ps 67:7; Ezek 34:27).

verses.translation: Brothers{H251}, if one{H259} among you goes{H1980} from the good{H2896} way{H1870} to evil{H7451}, and one{H259} turns him back{H4513},
Know{H3045} that whoever turns{H2015} him from his wickedness{H7564} saves{H5337} one{H259} soul{H5315} from death{H4194} and atones{H3722} for many{H7227} iniquities{H5771}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses mekhapper (atones, H3722 -- kaphar). This is the specific priestly atonement verb used for Yom Kippur (Lev 16:30, 23:28), the sin offering (Lev 4:20,26,31,35), and the scapegoat ritual. Greek has kalupsei (shall cover/hide). While kaphar also means to cover, the priestly atonement connotation is unique to Hebrew. A back-translator from generic kalupsei (cover) would not choose the loaded kaphar.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: mekhapper (atones, priestly term). Greek: kalupsei (covers/hides).
translation_notes: The closing verse frames the act of turning someone from sin in priestly/sacrificial terms -- it achieves atonement (kippurim).

chapter_notes.summary: James 5 in Hebrew contains some of the most decisive one-way markers in the epistle. Verse 4 directly alludes to Leviticus 19:13 with pe'ulat sachir shetalin (the wage of the hired worker that lodges overnight) -- the specific Torah prohibition against withholding wages. Verse 7 uses yoreh umalqosh (early and latter rain, from Deut 11:14, Joel 2:23) -- the precise Hebrew agricultural-calendar terms that Greek merely renders as early and late. Verse 5 uses ugav (pipe/organ, H5748) from Genesis 4:21 where Greek has a generic reference to luxury. Verse 11 combines a reference to Iyov (Job) with el rachamim verav chesed (God of compassion and abundant lovingkindness), echoing Exodus 34:6. Most strikingly, verse 16 quotes Psalm 145:18 VERBATIM: karov YHWH lekhol qor'av lekhol asher yiqra'uhu be'emet -- a Psalm quotation completely absent from the Greek, which instead has a generic proverb about effective prayer. Verse 3 uses acharit hayamim (end of days) -- the fixed Hebrew eschatological term. Verse 12 uses hen hen velav lav (yes yes and no no), mixing Hebrew and Aramaic naturally.
